units.text: Ask a class of twenty if they've ever copied homework. Anyone who did has a reason to say no. Only we can see the truth. Four of them did. So everyone flips a coin where nobody can see. Heads, tell the truth. Tails, flip a second coin, and let it answer. Heads for yes, tails for no.

On average, half the class tells the truth. Two of our four say yes. The other ten get the second coin. Five yes, five no, whatever the truth. Seven yes, thirteen no. That's all the survey sees. From those two numbers, how could the survey get back to four?

Take away the second coin's yeses. On average that's five, a quarter of the class. Two are left. Those two came from the half who told the truth. So double them. Four. No answer is a confession. But someone who copied says yes three times as often as someone who didn't.

Give every student all four coin outcomes, equally likely. Twenty students, eighty outcomes. Someone who copied says yes in three of their four. Someone who didn't, in one. Three times as likely. For a no, it's the reverse, three times again. So a student says yes. What's the chance they copied?

Count the yes outcomes. The four who copied have twelve, the sixteen others sixteen. Twelve of twenty-eight. On average, three of the seven yeses. Three in seven, not three in four. Each copier has three times the yeses, but the others outnumber them four to one. A no works the same way. Four of the fifty-two no outcomes are a copier's, one in thirteen.

A yes lifts the chance from one in five to three in seven. A no drops it to one in thirteen. The coin fixes the three times. Where the chance ends up depends on the class. An answer is deniable, but not meaningless. How well the survey counts is a separate question.
Real coins don't land on average. Ask the class eight times with fresh coins. Their estimates run from minus four to fourteen. Only one lands on four.
Now count every way the coins can land. Four to the twentieth, over a trillion, all equally likely. The estimates pile up around four, the true count. How often does a class land exactly on four?

About one class in five. And about one in eleven goes below zero. Below zero means fewer yeses than the second coin alone gives on average. Rounding those up to zero would push the average above four.

Every answer wobbles the same, whoever gives it. Twenty of them, doubled, miss by about four people. That's for this fixed class. Sample twenty from a big school instead, and who gets picked adds its own scatter. If one in five copied, matching a direct question's precision takes almost six times as many people.
